sections.h2: Who sends and collects a Warren County tax bill?
sections.html:
Warren County divides the job three ways, and all three offices answer calls on weekdays. The PVA sets the assessment, the sheriff mails the bill and takes the money, and the County Clerk inherits whatever is still open when April 15 ends.

  • PVA: 429 E. 10th Avenue, Bowling Green, KY 42101, phone (270) 843-3268 per the county's department list, open 8:00 to 4:30.
  • Sheriff: (270) 842-1633, with a tax inquiry page for looking up and paying a bill. The business office is open 8:00 to 4:30.
  • County Clerk: P.O. Box 478, Bowling Green, KY 42102, phone (270) 842-9416. The clerk's own site sends property tax and valuation questions to the PVA.

The sheriff's page cites KRS 134.140 and 160.500 as the basis for its role as collector of state, county, school and district taxes, which it then distributes to each authority.

sections.h2: What does the sheriff's 2026 payment schedule look like?
sections.html:
The sheriff's site laid out the 2026 dates and told owners to expect a bill in the first week of October. Each window follows the statewide calendar in KRS 134.015.

  • October 1 to November 1, 2026: 2 percent off.
  • November 2 to December 31, 2026: the amount on the bill.
  • January 2027: 5 percent more.
  • February 1 to April 15, 2027: 21 percent more, which rolls the 10 percent penalty and the sheriff's fee into one figure.

The 2026 discount window closed November 1, 2026. Paying online carries a cost: $1.50 for a card payment of $60.00 or less, 2.49 percent above that, and $1.50 per ACH or e-check payment. American Express is refused. The site refreshes after 7:00 pm on business days, so a Friday payment may not appear until Monday night. On a large bill, an ACH payment avoids the percentage.

sections.h2: Why do two Warren County neighbors pay different rates?
sections.html:
Warren County has two public school districts. Warren County Public Schools covers most of the county, including the outer parts of Bowling Green, while Bowling Green Independent Schools serves most of the city. The clerk's 2025 rate sheet shows how big that choice is: a city school levy of 84.80 cents against 52.20 cents for the county district.

The county levies add to 21.45 cents. Stacking them gives three combined rates: 84.25 outside a city, 104.55 inside a city but in the county school district, and 137.15 inside a city and its own school district. Ask the sheriff which combination your address pays.

sections.h2: What would the median Warren County house owe?
sections.html:
The Census midpoint for an owner occupied home is $258,000. Assuming an assessment at that figure, the three combined rates produce annual bills of roughly $2,173.65 in the unincorporated county, $2,697.39 in a city with county schools, and $3,538.47 in a city with its own school district. The gap of more than $1,300 between the first and the last is something a buyer will notice.

Assessments and sale prices rarely match, so treat these figures as a way to compare districts. A homeowner who qualifies for the $49,100 exemption pays on $208,900 instead, which saves about $413.67 a year at the 84.25 rate.

sections.h2: Which Warren County owners qualify for the homestead exemption?
sections.html:
The PVA handles claims from owners 65 and older and from owners classified as totally disabled. For 2025 and 2026 the exemption removes $49,100 from the assessment, and the application must be backed with documents such as a birth certificate, license or passport. The QuickFacts count of residents who are 65 or older is 14.2 percent.

A disability claim comes up for yearly renewal. Veterans with a service connected disability, and owners that Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems has found permanently and totally disabled, are the two exceptions.

sections.h2: How do I protest a Warren County assessment?
sections.html:
Schedule a conference with the PVA, because Kentucky treats it as the required first step, and the county directory gives (270) 843-3268. The tax roll sits open for thirteen days from the first Monday of May. A taxpayer who has met with the PVA then files at the County Clerk before the day after inspection ends.

  • Photos, insurance records, building costs and sales listings are the evidence the local board expects.
  • A paid representative must be an attorney, accountant, appraiser, broker or similar professional with written authority.
  • The board meets 25 to 35 days after inspection closes, for up to five days.

Written reasons accompany any decision to raise or lower a value.

sections.h2: What does the Warren County Clerk do with bills unpaid on April 15?
sections.html:
That evening the sheriff transfers every open bill, each becoming a certificate of delinquency with a lien. The clerk keeps accepting payment right up to the annual sale and publishes a PDF list of current delinquent parcels. The 2026 sale was set for August 26, 2026 at 9:00 am at 429 E 10th Ave, Suite 100, and buyers had to register by August 17. Both dates have passed.

After the transfer, costs layer on quickly. Interest runs 1 percent a month, the clerk takes 10 percent of tax, penalty and interest, and the county attorney takes 20 percent unless the bill clears in the first five business days. A $10 lien recording and release fee also applies. The lien stays with the land for as long as 11 years, so a seller should settle it at closing and ask the clerk for a release.

sections.h2: What else should a Warren County seller know about the county?
sections.html:
Warren was carved from Logan County in 1796 and is Kentucky's fifth most populous county, with Bowling Green as its seat. Barren River runs through the city, with the Green River marking the north edge. Interstate 65 and the Natcher Parkway, now I-165, turned a farming county into a manufacturing one in the 1960s and 1970s. Cities besides Bowling Green are Oakland, Plum Springs, Smiths Grove and Woodburn. Visitors know it for Western Kentucky University, Beech Bend Park, the Corvette assembly plant and the National Corvette Museum.

Growth shows in Census QuickFacts: 149,375 people in mid 2025, 11.0 percent above the 2020 base, and 1,453 building permits in 2025. Median gross rent is $1,002 and owners live in 55.6 percent of homes. Of Warren adults, 32.3 percent hold a bachelor's degree, and 10.4 percent of residents were born abroad.

Permits matter. The county's Division for Building Services, at 1141 State Street, covers everywhere except Bowling Green and Oakland, charges $0.15 per square foot with a $45 minimum, and sets a fine of at least $500 for work begun without a permit. Sheds from 120 square feet and all pools need one. Phone (270) 843-5360 to ask about a past project before you list.

faqs.q: Which office takes payment for Warren County property tax?
faqs.a: The Warren County Sheriff's Office takes it, at (270) 842-1633. Its tax inquiry page lets you look up and pay a bill, and the business office is open 8:00 to 4:30 on business days.

faqs.q: Did the 2026 Warren County discount end?
faqs.a: Yes. It ran from October 1 through November 1, 2026. The face amount applies through December 31, 2026, then a 5 percent penalty starts in January 2027.

faqs.q: Why is the Warren County school tax higher in some places?
faqs.a: The city school district levy is 84.80 cents per $100, against 52.20 cents for the county district, according to the clerk's 2025 rate sheet. Parcels inside the city's own district pay the higher one.

faqs.q: Does Warren County charge extra to pay by card?
faqs.a: Yes. A card payment costs $1.50 up to $60.00 and 2.49 percent above that. ACH and e-check payments cost $1.50, and American Express is not accepted.

faqs.q: How many people live in Warren County, Kentucky?
faqs.a: The Census estimate is 149,375 for July 2025. That is up 11.0 percent from the April 2020 base of 134,563, and the County Clerk's office calls Warren the fastest growing county in Kentucky.
